item.title: We know how to hurt India, says Pakistan coach Solano ahead of SAFF Championship final. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan head coach Nolberto Solano believes his side has what it takes to trouble India in the SAFF Championship final, insisting that his players must focus on their own strengths rather than become preoccupied with their opponents as the two arch-rivals prepare for a historic showdown on Tuesday.

Pakistan will face defending champions India at the National Stadium in Dhaka, Bangladesh, with the Green Shirts chasing their maiden SAFF Championship title and a landmark first appearance in the tournament’s final.

Speaking at the pre-match press conference on Monday, Solano acknowledged India’s quality but maintained that Pakistan had studied their opponents and understood where they could make an impact.

“We all prepare. It’s a final match, and we respect India. We are always checking and looking, but in football there are no more secrets,” Solano said.

“You know how they play. The most important thing is to focus on ourselves, on what we want to do, because we know our strengths and how we can hurt India.”

The Peruvian coach described the encounter as a special occasion and a derby, recognising the significance of a Pakistan-India contest, particularly with silverware at stake.

However, he stressed that his team’s attention must remain on executing its own game plan rather than allowing the occasion or the opposition to dictate its approach.

‘Football history’

For Pakistan, Tuesday’s final represents an opportunity to turn an encouraging tournament campaign into one of the most significant achievements in the country’s football history.

The Green Shirts booked their place in the showpiece match with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over hosts Bangladesh in Saturday’s semi-final. Abdul Samad Arshad scored the decisive goal in the closing stages to send Pakistan into their first-ever SAFF Championship final.

Their progress has been particularly noteworthy given the limited preparation time and the difficulties surrounding the availability of several overseas-based players during the group stage.

Pakistan’s final opponents, meanwhile, are pursuing a historic achievement of their own. India have won the SAFF Championship nine times and will be looking to secure an unprecedented third consecutive title, having lifted the trophy in the previous two editions.

The final will be a rematch of the Group ‘B’ encounter between the two sides on Nov 5, when India secured a 3-2 victory after establishing a commanding three-goal advantage.

Suhail Ahmad Bhat scored twice, while Manglenthang Kipgen added India’s third as Pakistan struggled to find their rhythm during the opening half.

The Green Shirts responded with two goals in stoppage time, including a spectacular overhead kick from Alamgir Ghazi, but their late rally proved insufficient to prevent defeat.

Solano admitted that Pakistan’s slow start and lack of concentration had contributed to the result, while also pointing to the difficult journey and inadequate preparation time before their opening fixture.

“I don’t like to make excuses, but we had a very bad journey before we arrived, and we faced them without two days of training. In the first 45 minutes, we weren’t focused. We were quite slow, so they took their chances and scored,” he said.

The coach, however, was encouraged by his side’s response after the interval, believing Pakistan had shown enough improvement to suggest they could compete more effectively in the rematch.

“In the second half, we improved and played much better. We could have come back into the match, but we did it a little bit late. That’s why we lost 3-2. But it’s another game, a different game,” Solano added.

Pakistan’s squad has since received a significant boost with the arrival of several overseas-based players who were unavailable during the group stage because the tournament fell outside the FIFA international window.

Captain Abdullah Iqbal, Easah Suliman, Adil Nabi, Ali Akbar Khan and Abdul Samad Arshad were among the players who joined the squad ahead of the knockout stages, giving Solano additional options and greater depth.

The impact of their arrival has been evident in Pakistan’s subsequent performances, particularly their defensive organisation and ability to manage difficult moments against Bangladesh.

India coach Naushad Moosa has also acknowledged that Pakistan present a different challenge from the team his side defeated in the group stage, pointing to the arrival of additional players and the tactical adjustments expected for the final.

‘Biggest achievement’

Abdullah acknowledged the importance of the occasion but insisted that the players would not approach the final any differently from their other matches.

Rather than allowing the pressure of a historic opportunity to affect their performance, the defender wants his teammates to remain disciplined, support one another and follow the instructions of the coaching staff.

“It’s a final, a big game, but we have to take it like any other game. Focus on the plan the coach has set for us, help each other out on the pitch and perform as usual. Nothing extra,” Abdullah said.

He admitted that the pressure of competing for a major regional title was unavoidable, particularly given what victory would mean for Pakistan football, but insisted that it would serve as additional motivation.

“Of course, there is pressure to win a final. It’s a big thing for our country, creating history, and it only motivates us to do better,” he added.

Abdullah also described Pakistan’s qualification for the final as a historic achievement, saying a tournament triumph would take the country’s footballing progress to another level.

“On the footballing side, it is the biggest achievement that we’re here in the final, and if we can go all the way, it will be even bigger,” the captain said.

With Pakistan having played a demanding schedule during the tournament, Solano was also asked whether fatigue could become a concern ahead of the final.

The coach dismissed the suggestion, insisting that his players were mentally prepared for the challenge and would not use the schedule as an excuse.

“Nobody is tired, my friend. We all focus. We all have a strong mentality,” he said. “When you play a final, my friends, the last thing you can be is tired. We are ready for fighting. No excuse. We want to give you everything.”

item.title: Zero tolerance for emboldened criminals. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The 30-minute rampage inside Durbin Bangla restaurant in Mohakhali, simply because an individual was asked to wait for a table, is simply unacceptable. That this escalated to assault of the staff, looting cash, ripping out CCTV hard drives, and inflicting up to Tk30 lakh in damages is infuriating.
That very same night, helmeted gunmen opened fire on Anurag Pharmacy on Mohammadpur's Babar Road -- barely 500 metres from a deputy police commissioner's office -- narrowly missing a sales employee’s head following repeated crude bomb blasts and an extortion demand.
Such incidents cannot be taken as isolated aberrations but rather must be seen as symptoms of a growing culture of impunity tightening and of criminals who have been emboldened due to a lack of consequences for their actions.
When armed extortionists can casually shoot up a busy storefront, and entitled thugs can systematically destroy a thriving restaurant in broad daylight without immediate consequences, the message sent to citizens and business owners is chilling: No one is safe, and criminals no longer fear the state.
What is most troubling is the sluggish, reactive posture of law enforcement. Routine assurances that "investigations are underway" are cold comfort to terrorized workers and entrepreneurs watching their livelihoods shattered.
The state cannot afford to turn a blind eye to escalating urban insecurity or treat violent extortion and mob vandalism as routine policing matters. Protecting life, property, and commercial activity is the most basic obligation of the state.
It’s time to enforce an uncompromising, zero-tolerance policy against street thuggery, political muscle-flexing, and armed extortion. Law enforcement too must hold negligent officers accountable for delayed interventions.
Our capital’s residents and businesses deserve a capital governed by the rule of law and not surrendered to the whims of vandals and gunmen.

item.title: Stop making citizens pay. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
To say that Bangladesh’s banking sector is being drowned by non-performing loans (NPLs) would be a laughable understatement at this point.
With the default loan rate hitting a staggering 32.78%, nearly one out of every three taka disbursed across the country's financial system is now non-performing.
Worse still, many analysts are saying what many have long feared: There is virtually zero chance of recovering 80-90% of these toxic assets.
That the overwhelming majority of this crisis is the direct result of operational failures, procedural sabotage, and outright financial crimes should leave every person in this country fuming.
While full-fledged Islamic banks stagger under a 58.9% default rate and state-owned lenders bleed at 43.2%, willful defaulters continue to exploit court injunctions, currently blocking the recovery of Tk 182,419 crore across 845 pending lawsuits to shield stolen public wealth.
It is entirely unacceptable that ordinary depositors, honest entrepreneurs, and taxpayers are continuously forced to absorb the consequences of such gross impunity.
When banks are starved of liquidity by corporate looters, legitimate businesses face suffocating borrowing costs. In addition, our private sector credit growth has collapsed to dismal lows, and savers continue to watch their hard-earned deposits trapped in dysfunctional institutions.
Tackling such a predicament has long been beyond the capacity of banks alone and the government and the central bank must do better. We must end this cycle of opaque half-measures and taxpayer-funded bailouts.
This starts with regular public disclosures on cash recoveries, capital adequacy, and above all, revealing the identities of top willful defaulters. In addition, independent audits and bank-specific resolution frameworks must be enforced without political interference.
Fixing the banking sector cannot mean endlessly penalizing the general public. The state must hold the ones who broke our banks accountable.

item.title: Is it the technology or its owners?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Sixty years ago, the idea of everyone having a video phone in their pocket was the stuff of science fiction.
That people might spend more time on devices doing things other than making actual phone calls would have seemed stranger still, but here we are. A world where fretting about the impact of our own and other peoples’ screen time on society is a more likely choice to make than going without a phone.
As with climate change, individual decisions and consumer choices count enough to make a difference, but most of the actual power to substantively improve regulations and standards rests with politicians and giant global corporations.
In the run-up to the US mid-term Congressional elections this month, Silicon Valley companies and their owners donated $600 million dollars to Republican candidates.
A large proportion of this came from Elon Musk spending about $200m on supporting Ken Paxton, the losing Republican candidate for a Senate seat in Texas.
Whilst the vast amounts given to Republican candidates did not prevent an anti-Trump wave of Democratic party successes, they reflect the growing amounts being spent by Silicon Valley titans on buying political influence.
Big Tech’s societal and environmental footprint and its record of abusing monopolistic positions, aggressively minimizing paying taxes, failing to safeguard privacy, and designing algorithms to addict users and profit from amplifying political extremes and other harmful content already raises many ethical questions. Yet, the latest spending added to the concerns about its political lobbying and future trajectory.
Moore’s law, named after a co-founder of Intel, observed that the number of transistors it is technically possible to fit onto an integrated circuit can be doubled every two years at little increase in cost. For decades it was this rate of exponential improvement that enabled ever more computing power to be made available at lower prices to ordinary consumers.
In turn, these underpinned bigger projections and valuations for the sector. In 2016, the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization was Apple with the aggregate value of its shares peaking above $500bn.
Ten years on, its value is ten times larger at $5 trillion. This is different from being the world’s largest company by actual revenue; Apple’s revenues place it as only the seventh largest company.
Apple’s stock market value reflects the willingness of investors to bet on the tech sector’s future growth. Since 2020 this optimism has become based less on Moore’s law delivering cost reductions for consumers -- its effect is slowing down as semiconductor manufacturers adjust to the growing complexity and cost of making ever smaller circuits just as global supply chains have fragmented -- and more on a belief in future profits from AI.
Potential impacts of AI, both positive and negative, are easy enough to imagine, given the pace of change the sector is promising. Predictions of technological dystopias and utopias are a hardy staple of speculative fiction.
Right now, AI has an insatiable appetite for capital investment in scaling up computational power and data centres. These are demanding ever greater amounts of electricity and water for cooling systems.
The cost neutral arithmetic of energy costs remaining stable as computer chips and systems become smaller and more powerful promised by Moore’s law has been turned completely upside down by a globalized gold rush to grow AI.
Even in a world that had free energy, this direction of travel would be controversial given the sector’s impact on jobs, but in a world with a growing population seeking to cut carbon emissions, amid plenty of pre-existing concerns about Big Tech, it is politically toxic.
Seen in this light, the sectors’ growing political donations and lobbying efforts on AI, not just in the United States, but in countries around the world, are easy to explain.
Like other industries, it wants to keep pipelines of investment flowing and persuade politicians to support them with financial incentives and favourable laws.
But what if it is all just snake oil and a digital Ponzi scheme?
Scepticism is a rational stance given the vast scope and impact of the IT sector. But even where politicians seek to regulate aspects of the sector, their actions tend to be limited or seem like locking a stable door after the horse has bolted.
Given that parts of the sector like digital cryptocurrencies were designed to be largely decentralized and unregulated in nature, such naivete is troubling given that aspects of it can be used to enable criminality.
Dogmatic faith in future growth and cultish attitudes towards IT founders and products abound around the sector and among many consumers. Perhaps not surprisingly, many of the biggest critics of the ownership structures and strategies of the sector come from within its highly educated workforce and support the open-source movement.
Of course, the argument that technology is simply a tool that can be used for good or bad is ostensibly an objective one.
But when those making it are tech giants with monopolistic tendencies that stand to profit either way, calls for democratic scrutiny, breaking up monopolies, public accountability, and for that matter public ownership, all deserve to be heard.
It’s the oligarchs, stupid.
Niaz Alam is London Bureau Chief, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Calling out the digital inquisitors. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In the interconnected landscape of modern South Asia, the digital square was once heralded as a beacon of democratic expression. Today, however, it increasingly resembles a medieval plaza where a baying mob gathers, stones in hand, waiting for the next target to be dragged into the light.
Across India, Pakistan, and the wider region, whenever tragedy strikes or a viral controversy erupts, a familiar and sickening ritual unfolds online. Behind a shroud of anonymous handles, inactive profile pictures, and automated bot networks, a pervasive strain of digital chauvinism rears its head.
These faceless commentators rush with predatory speed to demean, judge, and ultimately blame women for their own suffering.
Whether it is a high-profile criminal case of rape and murder, a domestic abuse tragedy, or a viral public misstep, the verdict from this digital jury is always preemptive and predictable: The woman is guilty.
This phenomenon is not merely an annoyance of modern internet culture; it is a profound social rot.
It reveals a deep-seated, short-sighted misogyny that weaponizes human suffering to reinforce archaic prejudices, demanding that we confront and socially shun these insidious behaviours before they erode the moral fabric of our societies.
The anatomy of victim-blaming
The most harrowing manifestation of this online malice occurs in the wake of heinous crimes -- rapes, assaults, and murders that shock the public conscience.
In a just society, a horrific crime against a woman should provoke universal outrage, sorrow, and an uncompromising demand for justice against the perpetrator.
Yet, in the virtual echo chambers of South Asia, the narrative is routinely subverted.
When a woman is attacked or killed, the digital inquisitors immediately pivot away from the perpetrator’s guilt to dissect the victim’s life with microscopic scrutiny.
Why was she out alone at night? Where was her male guardian or family member? What was she wearing?
In cases involving minors, the depravity sinks even lower, with commentators bizarrely projecting adult anxieties onto children, questioning their clothing or presence in public spaces as if to rationalize the unrationalizable.
This is the quintessence of victim-blaming. It is a psychological defense mechanism rooted in a fragile worldview that cannot bear the thought of a chaotic, dangerous world where women are independent agents.
By blaming the victim, these commentators construct a comforting illusion of control: “If she hadn’t done X, Y, or Z, she would have been safe.”
In doing so, they absolve the actual criminal and place the burden of virtue and safety entirely on the shoulders of women.
It sends a chilling message to half the population: Your safety is conditional, and if you step outside the narrow parameters dictated by society, your tragedy is your own fault.
Attire, liberty, and the ‘liberal mind’
Beyond violent crimes, everyday viral controversies draw the same predatory swarm.
Let a video surface of a woman making a mistake in public, navigating a personal dispute, or simply living her life on her own terms, and the social media comment sections transform into cesspools of moral panic.
Here, the faceless profiles deploy a standard checklist of grievances.
Every complex socio-economic issue, every cultural shift, and every personal failure is summarily blamed on "indecent attire," "polygamous behaviour" (often invoked as a catch-all insult), and the dreaded "liberal mind."
If a woman exercises agency over her life, her career, or her relationships, she is immediately branded as a corrupting influence on traditional values.
The underlying rhetoric is transparently hypocritical: Men can indulge in every conceivable excess without denting their moral standing, but a woman’s entire character is judged by a single snapshot, a rumour, or a manipulated video clip.
Commentators jump on these bandwagons without a second thought for context, nuance, or basic human empathy.
Facts do not matter to the mob. Once the narrative is set -- that women have become too "modern," too "independent," and too "uncontrolled" -- the digital machinery of character assassination goes into overdrive.
From faceless bots to female envy
What makes this digital ecosystem particularly toxic is its composition.
It is propelled not just by men hiding behind pseudonyms, but also by a distinct psychological undercurrent of internalized misogyny.
On one hand, we have the legions of nameless male profiles -- the virtual moral police whose own lives are often defined by frustration, stagnation, and a deep-seated insecurity regarding modern, autonomous women.
Their online vitriol is an outlet for impotent rage against a changing world where women refuse to remain silent, subservient second-class citizens.
Protected by the anonymity of a screen, these men project their anxieties onto viral targets, seeking a toxic sense of community and validation from other like-minded misogynists.
On the other hand, we must confront an uncomfortable truth: This phenomenon is not exclusively male.
Often, women themselves participate in the shaming, driven by a potent mix of social conditioning and deep-seated envy. In societies where female worth has historically been tied to strict conformity, seeing another woman break the mold can trigger a defensive reaction.
Some women, having internalized patriarchal standards to survive, view independent or non-conformist women as a threat to the fragile security they have carved out for themselves.
By joining the mob, they signal their own "purity" and conformity. This betrayal from within is perhaps the most tragic aspect of the cycle, as it fractures solidarity precisely when it is needed most.
Call for social ostracization
We have reached a critical juncture in the digital evolution of South Asia. The line between online commentary and real-world harm has long since blurred.
When internet trolls normalize victim-blaming, they create a cultural climate where violence against women is minimized, excused, or implicitly encouraged.
This behaviour cannot simply be brushed aside as "just internet noise" or the ramblings of "trolls being trolls."
These voices shape public perception, intimidate survivors into silence, and deter women from seeking justice or participating fully in public life.
Combating this requires a fundamental cultural reset.
We must strip away the digital armour that emboldens these cowards.
Anonymity on social media should no longer be a free pass to terrorize victims of crime or ruin reputations with impunity.
Platforms must be held accountable for enabling networks of abuse and algorithmic amplification of misogyny.
More importantly, the remedy must come from society itself.
These shamelessly insensitive remarks and baseless accusations must be actively confronted and socially shunned.
Just as we would condemn someone for making excuses for a thief or a murderer in a physical room, we must call out those who excuse abuse and degradation in the digital room.
Friends, family members, colleagues, and community leaders must make it clear that victim-blaming and casual misogyny are not "opinions" to be debated -- they are moral failures.
Until the cost of participating in online harassment becomes too high -- until social circles, workplaces, and public platforms make it socially untenable to bully and blame women -- the digital public square will remain a dangerous frontier.
It is time to drag these faceless inquisitors out of the shadows and hold them to the light of accountability.
Women in our society deserve nothing less than a culture that protects their dignity, respects their autonomy, and refuses to negotiate with the malice of the mob.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.
